<reason>B won the central clash: requiring consent does not make consent sufficient for legality or override stronger prohibitions. A’s dark-pattern and coercion objections established genuine limitations, but B answered them directly and explained the additional protection for people who never authorize sales. A’s eventual blanket-minimization alternative supplied no convincing reason to reject this minimum requirement. Its late political-crowding prediction was unsupported, while its closing repeated the already-damaged claim that the motion licenses dangerous sales. B offered the clearer textual interpretation and comparative enforcement case.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s pressure question exposed the unsupported claim that consent provides a “lawful pathway around” use bans. A conceded that nothing overrides those bans, then shifted to their absence from the motion. B decisively answered that prohibiting sales without consent does not require permitting sales with consent.</best_rebuttal>
